entries.title: MURCH-ZAWY VULNERABILITY
entries.body:
A theoretical attack on Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism, described by Zawy and formalized by Murch (Mark Erhardt) in August 2024. Unlike the classic *time warp* attack, this vulnerability does not exploit the *off-by-one* error in the calculation of the duration of retarget periods, but relies on the strategic alternation of timestamps at the last block of each difficulty period.

The attacker, who controls a majority of the computing power, keeps timestamps at the minimum allowed by the *Median Time Past* (MTP) rule during each period, then sets the timestamp of the last block far in the future to reduce the difficulty by a factor of 4. By then alternating between a minimal timestamp and a future timestamp for the last blocks of each period, they make the difficulty oscillate between a quarter and a sixteenth of the initial value. Some periods then show a negative calculated duration, but the protocol treats it as half a week, which raises the difficulty only by a factor of 4.

In practice, the attack requires about 16 weeks of selfish mining. At the end of this period, the attacker publishes their secret chain, reorganizes about 8,064 blocks and collects the rewards of about 39,816 blocks. Murch proposed a variant that reduces the difficulty exponentially by increasing the future timestamp in steps.

BIP-0054 (Consensus Cleanup) fixes this vulnerability by requiring that the timestamp of the last block of a difficulty period be greater than or equal to that of the first block of the same period.

entries.title: VALENCY
entries.body: In the RGB protocol, a *Valency* designates a public right that does not require the explicit storage of a state, but that can later be redeemed via a *State Extension*. This mechanism is a possibility declared beforehand in the contract logic, accessible to everyone or to specific actors, and it allows a specific extension of the contract state to be triggered when the defined conditions are met. The *Valency* thus offers a flexible and modular solution for anticipating future changes to the contract.

entries.title: VALIDATIONLESS MINING
entries.body: A mining practice that consists of starting work on a new candidate block as soon as the hash of the previous block's header is received, without having downloaded or verified all of its transactions. Also called *SPV mining*, this method lets the miner gain a few seconds over those who wait for full validation of the block before starting their own work.

entries.title: VALUE OVERFLOW INCIDENT
entries.body:
A bug exploited on August 15, 2010 on the Bitcoin network, which led to the creation of more than 184 billion bitcoins in a single transaction. The attacker exploited an integer overflow (*integer overflow*) vulnerability in the amount verification: two outputs of 92,233,720,368.54 BTC each, close to the maximum representable by a signed 64-bit integer, caused an overflow during the addition, which produced a positive result below the detection threshold.

The problem was quickly spotted by Jeff Garzik, who alerted the community on the BitcoinTalk forum. Satoshi Nakamoto published a fix within hours. This fix added an explicit check of each output amount as well as of their sum, and rejected any transaction that contained negative or excessive values. Miners then adopted the new version of the software and produced an alternative chain that excluded the invalid transaction.

The corrected chain overtook the chain containing the bug at block 74,691, after about 53 blocks of disruption. This episode, recorded under the identifier CVE-2010-5139, is the first major incident in the history of Bitcoin and led to the implementation of the network alert system.

entries.title: VANITY ADDRESS
entries.body: A custom receiving address that contains a specific sequence of characters chosen by the user, generally for aesthetic reasons. These addresses are generated by running a computational process, in which many private keys are created until one of them corresponds to a receiving address containing the desired sequence. This process does not compromise the security of the address, but it can require considerable computing time and resources, especially for longer or more specific sequences. It is a kind of *brute force* process.

entries.title: VANITYGEN
entries.body: The first open source command-line software used to create custom receiving addresses (*vanity address*). It works by generating and testing key pairs by trial and error until a receiving address matching the criteria specified by the user (such as a certain sequence of specific characters) is found. Vanitygen requires an intensive computational process, particularly for long sequences.

entries.title: VARIANCE
entries.body:
In the context of mining, designates the fluctuations in a miner's income due to the probabilistic nature of the search for valid blocks. Even with constant computing power, the time needed to find a block can vary considerably. Consequently, miners can go through long periods without receiving rewards, followed by periods of substantial gains.

Mining pools are designed to reduce this variance. By pooling the computing power of many individual hashers, pools increase the frequency at which blocks are found, which allows a more regular and predictable distribution of rewards. The variance is thus said to be reduced.

Variance is an inherent flaw of Bitcoin's proof-of-work mechanism that pushes toward the grouping of mining.

entries.title: VAULT
entries.body:
An advanced security mechanism for holding bitcoins, based on a two-step spending process that imposes a delay between the announcement of a withdrawal and its actual execution. In the first transaction, the user signals their intention to move the funds. A waiting period then elapses, during which the legitimate owner can detect any theft attempt and redirect the funds to a secure recovery address ("*clawback*"). If no intervention takes place, a second transaction finalizes the transfer.

Several technical approaches have been proposed to implement vaults. The first relies on presigned transactions: the spending transactions are signed in advance, then the signing keys are destroyed in order to guarantee that only the predefined paths remain usable. This method requires no modification of the protocol, but it demands rigorous management of key destruction. The second approach, more elegant, relies on covenants, that is, constraints applied directly in scripts to limit the way a UTXO can be spent. The proposal `OP_VAULT`, formalized in BIP-0345, introduces dedicated opcodes (`OP_VAULT` and `OP_VAULT_RECOVER`) that considerably simplify the construction of vaults at the consensus level, but this proposal was abandoned in favor of `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY`, which is more general-purpose.

Vaults are particularly suited to institutional cold storage, where security takes precedence over speed of access to the funds.

entries.title: VBYTES
entries.body:
A unit of measurement used to evaluate the size of a Bitcoin transaction while taking into account the weighting introduced by SegWit. A vByte (virtual byte) represents a normalized weight unit: 4 weight units (WU) correspond to 1 vByte. This measurement makes it possible to fairly compare SegWit transactions and *legacy* transactions.

Before SegWit, the size of a transaction was measured in raw bytes. With SegWit, witness data (*witness*) benefit from a discount: each witness byte counts for 1 WU, versus 4 WU for other data. Calculating in vBytes smooths out this difference. For example, a transaction whose total weight is 600 WU is 150 vBytes.

Transaction fees are calculated in satoshis per vByte (sat/vB). Using vBytes allows wallets to correctly estimate fees regardless of the structure of the transaction. A Bitcoin block can contain a maximum of 4 million WU, equivalent to 1 million vBytes.

entries.title: VERSIONING
entries.body: In the context of Bitcoin, designates the process of assigning specific versions to various elements of the protocol, in order to facilitate their tracking, management and updating. Versions are numbered sequentially, making it possible to identify the changes made, new features or bug fixes. For example, each block of the blockchain contains a version number, indicating the consensus rules and data structures applied when it was created. Versioning exists for script types, for transactions, for blocks, for the Bitcoin Core software, for network communications...

entries.title: VEXL
entries.body:
An open source mobile application that allows buying and selling bitcoin peer-to-peer, without identity verification (KYC). Launched in 2022, Vexl is operated by the Vexl Foundation, a nonprofit organization supported by SatoshiLabs, the company behind Trezor.

The application relies on an original principle: counterparties are discovered through the user's social graph, that is, their phone contacts and the contacts of their contacts. This mechanism digitally reproduces the trust of in-person exchanges.

All communications are end-to-end encrypted, no personal data is stored, and each public profile is unique to each transaction.

entries.title: VIABTC
entries.body: A Bitcoin mining pool founded in 2016 in China. ViaBTC is among the main mining pools in the world in terms of hashrate. It stands out for the diversity of its payout methods: PPS+, PPLNS and *solo mining*, allowing miners to choose the model best suited to their risk profile.

entries.title: VIN
VIRGIN BITCOIN
entries.body: A unit of bitcoin freshly issued in a coinbase transaction (block reward) and that has never yet been spent in a subsequent transaction. Its transaction history is therefore free of any association with activities identified by chain analysis tools.

entries.title: VLS
entries.body:
Acronym for "Validating Lightning Signer". An open source library in Rust that separates the private keys of a Lightning node from the node software itself, moving them to a dedicated signing device. Before each cryptographic operation, VLS applies a set of more than fifty validation rules to verify that the proposed transaction is safe.

If the node is compromised or attempts a malicious action, such as signing a revoked *commitment transaction* or closing a channel to an unauthorized address, VLS refuses the signature. This mechanism protects the funds even in the event of total compromise of the node software.

VLS offers reference integrations for CLN and LDK. The project is still in active development and has not reached the stage of a stable production release.

entries.title: VOLATILITY
entries.body: A measure of the amplitude of an asset's price variations over a given period. In the context of Bitcoin, volatility designates the sometimes significant fluctuations of the BTC price relative to fiat currencies such as the dollar or the euro. High volatility means that the price can experience sharp rises or falls in a short time.

entries.title: VOLTAGE
entries.body:
A cloud infrastructure platform dedicated to the Lightning Network. Voltage allows businesses and developers to deploy and manage Lightning nodes (LND, Core Lightning) without having to administer the underlying infrastructure.

The platform offers node hosting, monitoring tools and liquidity management services. These features make it easier to integrate the Lightning Network into commercial applications.

Voltage's model is non-custodial: the node operator retains control of their keys and funds.

entries.title: VOUT
entries.body:
A specific element of a Bitcoin transaction that determines the destination of the funds sent. A transaction can include several outputs, each one distinctly identified by the combination of the transaction identifier (`txid`) and an index called `vout`. This index, which starts at `0`, marks the position of the output in the sequence of the transaction's outputs. Thus, the first output will be designated by `"vout": 0`, the second by `"vout": 1`, and so on.

Each `vout` mainly encapsulates two pieces of information:
* the value, expressed in bitcoins, which represents the amount sent;
* a locking script (`scriptPubKey`) that stipulates the conditions required for the funds to be spent again in a subsequent transaction.

The combination of the `txid` and the `vout` of a specific coin forms what is called an *outpoint*, for example:

* txid:

```
4c160086e39a940c2459f03bb7cfe5b768fc78373c9960dc2cf2fa61b57d0adf
```

* vout:

```
0
```

* outpoint:

```
4c160086e39a940c2459f03bb7cfe5b768fc78373c9960dc2cf2fa61b57d0adf:0
```

entries.title: VPRV
entries.body: Extended private key prefix for SegWit V0 accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

entries.title: VPUB
entries.body: Extended public key prefix for SegWit V0 accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

entries.title: VTXO
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Virtual Transaction Output*". A VTXO is a virtual share of an on-chain Bitcoin UTXO within the Ark protocol. Rather than each owning an individual UTXO on the blockchain (costly in fees and hard to scale), several users share a single UTXO via VTXOs managed by an *Ark Service Provider* (ASP).

A VTXO is obtained either by depositing on-chain bitcoin to a boarding address (*boarding address*), or by receiving it from another user of the same ASP. VTXOs are atomically connected to one another: when Alice sends a VTXO to Bob, the ASP creates an on-chain output including Alice's share intended for Bob. Alice only loses her funds if Bob actually receives them. Existing VTXOs are continuously destroyed and recreated during rounds organized by the ASP.

VTXOs have an expiration date (typically 4 weeks). The user must refresh them before the deadline, otherwise the ASP recovers the liquidity. At any time, the user can perform a unilateral on-chain exit to convert their VTXO into a regular UTXO, although this operation involves transaction fees.
